title: Governance at the Union Level
summary: The Union government works on the parliamentary system. The executive is the President and the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister; the legislature is Parliament (President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha); the judiciary is headed by the Supreme Court. India is a republic because its Head of State is elected, not hereditary.

Election: indirectly, by an Electoral College of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and of the State Legislative Assemblies (including Delhi and Puducherry), by secret ballot, using proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote. Qualifications: citizen of India, at least 35 years old, qualified to be a member of the Lok Sabha, holding no office of profit. Term: five years; can be re-elected. A vacancy arises by death, resignation or removal by impeachment (a resolution passed by a special majority in both Houses for violation of the Constitution). The Vice-President then acts as President for not more than six months. Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the first President; Pratibha Patil the first woman President. The official residence is Rashtrapati Bhavan.

Powers: (a) Executive — appoints the Prime Minister (leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha) and other ministers on the PM's advice; Governors, the Attorney General, the Comptroller and Auditor General, ambassadors, the UPSC, the Chief Justice and judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, and the Election Commission; is Supreme Commander of the armed forces; treaties are made in his/her name. (b) Legislative — part of Parliament; addresses it, summons and prorogues the Houses, dissolves the Lok Sabha, calls a joint sitting, nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha; no bill becomes law without his/her assent; issues ordinances when Parliament is not in session (they lapse if not approved within six weeks of Parliament meeting). (c) Financial — no money bill without his/her recommendation; the budget is laid before the Lok Sabha with his/her consent. (d) Judicial — can pardon, suspend or reduce sentences.

Emergency powers: (i) National emergency for war, external aggression or armed rebellion — proclaimed only on the written decision of the Union Cabinet headed by the PM; must be approved by Parliament within one month; the Centre can direct the States and Fundamental Rights may be suspended (declared in 1962, 1965, 1971 and 1975). (ii) President's Rule (Article 356) when the constitutional machinery in a State fails — approved within two months, lasts six months at a time and at most three years; the Governor runs the State and Parliament makes its laws; misuse was checked by the S.R. Bommai case (1994). (iii) Financial emergency — never declared so far.

Position: the President is the constitutional (nominal) head; he/she must act on the binding advice of the Council of Ministers, though he/she can ask it to reconsider once. Dr. Ambedkar compared the office to the British monarch — the President represents the nation but does not rule it. Yet the President is not a rubber stamp: he/she preserves and defends the Constitution and can play a decisive role when no party has a majority.
## Prime Minister and Council of Ministers

The President appoints as Prime Minister the leader of the majority (a party or coalition) in the Lok Sabha, who must become an MP within six months. The PM is the real head of the Union executive: recommends ministers and allocates portfolios, presides over the Cabinet, is the link between the President and the Council of Ministers, can advise dissolution of the Lok Sabha, is the leader of Parliament and the nation, chairs the Planning Commission (now NITI Aayog) and the National Development Council, and represents India abroad. If the PM resigns, the whole Council goes. The PM is called the 'keystone of the cabinet arch'; in coalition governments (since 1977 at the Centre) he/she must be diplomatic with partners.

The Council of Ministers has three ranks — Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers. It is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha: if a no-confidence motion is passed, the whole Council must resign ('they swim and sink together') — as Vajpayee's government did in 1999.

Lok Sabha (House of the People): maximum 550 elected members (530 from States, 20 from Union Territories), directly elected by citizens aged 18 and above from territorial constituencies; term five years (can be dissolved earlier, extended by one year in emergency). Members must be citizens, 25 years old, without an office of profit. It is presided over by the Speaker, elected by members, who keeps order, decides who speaks, votes only in a tie, decides whether a bill is a money bill and presides over joint sittings.

Rajya Sabha (Council of States): maximum 250 members — 238 elected by State Legislative Assemblies by proportional representation, and 12 nominated by the President for literature, art, science and social service. It is a permanent house; members serve six years and one-third retire every two years. Minimum age 30. The Vice-President is its ex-officio Chairman. The Vice-President is elected by members of both Houses.

Functions: (i) Legislative — makes laws on the Union and Concurrent Lists and residuary subjects; deadlocks on ordinary bills are settled by a joint sitting where the Lok Sabha dominates. (ii) Control over the executive — Question Hour, calling-attention, adjournment and censure motions, and the no-confidence motion (Lok Sabha only). (iii) Financial — custodian of public money; no tax or expenditure without its approval; money bills start in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha can only recommend within 14 days. (iv) Judicial — fixes the number of judges and removes judges by impeachment. (v) Others — impeaches the President, removes the Vice-President, amends the Constitution and takes part in electing the President and Vice-President. The Lok Sabha is more powerful, but the Rajya Sabha is not merely a 'secondary chamber': only it can create a new All-India Service or let Parliament legislate on a State subject.
Union schemes affect daily life: ICDS anganwadis, Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, Rashtriya Madhyamik Shiksha Abhiyan, National Rural Health Mission, Total Sanitation Campaign, MGNREGA and Indira Awas Yojana.

India has a unified (single, integrated) judiciary with the Supreme Court at the top. It has a Chief Justice and other judges (the number is fixed by Parliament; 7 in 1950, 30 when the textbook was written). Judges are appointed by the President after consulting the Chief Justice and a collegium. Qualifications: citizen; five years as a High Court judge, or ten years as a High Court advocate, or a distinguished jurist in the President's opinion. They retire at 65 and can be removed only by impeachment for proved misbehaviour or incapacity; after retirement they cannot practise in any court.

Jurisdiction: original (disputes between the Union and States or between States); appellate (appeals in constitutional, civil and criminal cases from High Courts; special leave to appeal); advisory (opinion on questions referred by the President — not binding). It is a court of record, the guardian of the Constitution and protector of Fundamental Rights, and has the power of judicial review — declaring unconstitutional laws or orders null and void. Judicial activism, through Public Interest Litigation (PIL) which lets anyone petition on behalf of the poor or disadvantaged, has given judgments on pollution, child labour and illegal buildings; the public supports it because it gives the disadvantaged access to justice.

vsa: Explain the number of judges, including the Chief Justice, in the Supreme Court of India.

(1) As provided in the Constitution, the Supreme Court of India consists of the Chief Justice and other Judges whose number is prescribed by the Parliament from time to time. The Chief Justice and other Judges are appointed by the President. (2) In 1950 there was a Chief Justice and 7 judges; the number has been increased with need — the textbook gives a Chief Justice and 30 judges.
Explain the importance of a no-confidence motion in the Indian Parliament in two points.

(1) If the Lok Sabha passes a ‘no-confidence motion’, the entire Council of Ministers including PM has to resign. (2) It means that if they lose the confidence of the Lok Sabha, the Council of Ministers is dislodged with the resignation of the Prime Minister.
Mention any two qualifications required to be elected as President of India.

(1) To be eligible to be a member of the Rajya Sabha, a person must (a) be a citizen of India, and (b) be at least 30 years of age. (ii) (a) be a citizen of India (b) have completed the age of 35 years (c) be qualified for being elected as a Member of Lok Sabha (d) not hold any office of profit (2) (iii) be qualified for being elected as a member of the House of the People (Lok Sabha); and (iv) not hold any office of profit under the government of India, any State government or under any local authority or any other authority of the said government.
Describe any two powers of the Prime Minister related to the Council of Ministers.

(1) No money bill can be introduced in the Lok Sabha without his/her prior recommendation. But in practice, it is the Prime Minister who makes and unmakes the Council of Ministers. It is on his/ her recommendations that the President appoints the members of the Council of Ministers and distributes portfolios among them. (2) He/She presides over the meetings of the Cabinet and communicates its decisions to the President. If, due to any reason, he/she submits his/her resignation, the entire Council of Ministers stands dissolved.
How do both Houses of Parliament maintain control over the Council of Ministers? Highlight two ways.

(1) (a) By asking questions and supplementary questions: The first hour of every working day of Parliament relates to Question Hour in which the Ministers have to answer the questions raised by the members. (d) (i) ask questions and supplementary questions, (ii) adjournment motion and calling attention (2) (b) By discussing and passing motions: Calling Attention Motion, Adjournment Motion or Censure Motion can be moved and policies of the government can be debated and criticized. But only the Lok Sabha has the power to pass a no-confidence motion which if done, the Council of Minister resigns.
Differentiate between direct and indirect elections in India with examples.

The members of the Lok Sabha are directly elected by the people of India. He/She is indirectly elected by an Electoral College consisting of the elected members of both the Houses of the Parliament and the State Legislative Assemblies.
sa: Explain any three executive powers of the President of India.

(1) All executive actions of the government of India are carried out in his/her name. He/She also appoints other members of the Council of Ministers on the recommendations of the Prime Minister. (2) Appoints Governors, the Attorney General, the CAG, ambassadors, the UPSC, the Chief Justice and judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts and Election Commissioners, and can remove many of them as provided. (3) Moreover, the President is the supreme commander of the Armed Forces and appoints the Chiefs of the three wings, Army, Airforce and Navy. All diplomatic work is conducted and all international treaties and agreements are negotiated and concluded in his/her name.
Explain the functions of the Prime Minister.

(1) It is on his/ her recommendations that the President appoints the members of the Council of Ministers and distributes portfolios among them. He/She presides over the meetings of the Cabinet and communicates its decisions to the President. (2) All decisions are taken by the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister acts as the link between the President and the Council of Ministers. The Rajya Sabha is not subject to dissolution. (3) Leads Parliament and the nation, defends government policy, chairs the Planning Commission/NITI Aayog and NDC, and represents India abroad.
Explain the emergency powers of the President of India.

(1) National emergency for war, external aggression or armed rebellion — only on the Cabinet's written decision; approved by Parliament within a month; the Centre can direct States and Fundamental Rights may be suspended. (2) President's Rule (Art. 356) when a State's constitutional machinery fails — the Governor rules on the President's behalf and Parliament legislates for the State; maximum three years. (3) (iii) The third type of emergency, which is called ‘financial emergency’ is declared when a situation arises whereby the financial stability or credit of India or of any part of the country is threatened. In this situation, the President can reduce the salaries of all the government officials including the judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts. The financial emergency has not been proclaimed in India so far.
Explain the financial powers of the President of India.

(1) No money bill can be introduced in the Lok Sabha without his/her prior recommendation. (2) The President gives his consent for it to be laid before the Lok Sabha before the beginning of every financial year. As regards the Annual Budget (Annual Financial Statement), it is presented in the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha may only discuss it but can not stop it from becoming law. (3) In this situation, the President can reduce the salaries of all the government officials including the judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts. The financial emergency has not been proclaimed in India so far.
Describe the close relationship between the legislature and the executive in India.

(1) The executive (PM and ministers) are members of Parliament and must become MPs within six months. (2) The Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President, but they cannot be removed so long as they have the support of the majority in the Lok Sabha, In fact, according to the Constitution, Ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. But only the Lok Sabha has the power to pass a no-confidence motion which if done, the Council of Minister resigns. The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. (3) Parliament controls the executive through Question Hour, motions and approval of the budget, while the PM can advise the President to dissolve the Lok Sabha.
Explain the functions (jurisdiction) of the Supreme Court of India.

(1) The Prime Minister acts as the link between the President and the Council of Ministers. The Supreme Court has three types of jurisdiction— Original, Appellate and Advisory. the one side and one or more States on the other side. (2) The Supreme Court is a court of appeal for constitutional, civil and criminal cases. It can hear appeals against the judgments of the High Courts. (3) The President may also order the suspension of the enforcement of fundamental rights. (iii) Advisory Jurisdiction: The Supreme Court has a special advisory jurisdiction in matters which may specifically be referred to it by the President of India. The Supreme Court has the powers to interpret the Constitution, and through this it has assumed the power of judicial review. It functions as the guardian of the Constitution.

(2) He/She summons and prorogues the sessions of Parliament and can dissolve the Lok Sabha on the advice of the Council of Ministers. He/She is elected by an electoral college which consists of the members of both Houses of the Parliament. (3) Dissolves the Lok Sabha- When the President dissolves the Lok Sabha, it means that the House ceases to exist till it is reconstituted after the next elections. (4) The President addresses the Parliament every year at the commencement of the first session and after each general election to the Lok Sabha. If the Rajya Sabha along with its recommendations (if any) does not return it to Lok Sabha within 14 days, the bill is deemed to have been passed by both the Houses. (6) Calls a joint sitting to resolve deadlocks, issues ordinances when Parliament is not in session, and nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha.

la: Describe the functions of the Indian Parliament.

(1) Legislative: makes laws on the Union and Concurrent Lists and residuary subjects; joint sitting for deadlocks. (2) Control over the executive: Question Hour, motions and the no-confidence motion. (3) Financial: passes the budget; no tax or expenditure without its approval; money bills start in the Lok Sabha. (4) (iv) Judicial Functions: The Parliament is empowered to prescribe the number of Judges of the Supreme Court by law. His/Her term of office is for five years, though he/she can be removed even before through impeachment. (5) (b) Legislative Powers: The President is an integral part of the Parliament and in this capacity he/she enjoys many legislative powers. He/She is elected by an electoral college which consists of the members of both Houses of the Parliament. It participates in the election of the President and elects the Vice President of India. (6) Constituent: amends the Constitution and impeaches the President.
